Algebra 1 | Quarter 2 | Unit 3: Linear Relationships

Gear Up: Proportional Relationships

Does twice the pedaling mean twice the distance?

Duration
50 minutes
Grade level
Grades 8–9
Topic
Proportional Relationships
Standards
7.RP.A.2, 8.EE.B.5, HSA-CED.A.2

Students identify proportional relationships (y = kx) from tables, graphs and situations, find the constant of proportionality, and use gear ratios to see proportion in action.

2Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  • Decide whether a relationship is proportional using a table, a graph or an equation.
  • Find the constant of proportionality k = yx.
  • Write and use an equation of the form y = kx.
  • Explain why a linear relationship with a starting amount is not proportional.

3Essential question

When does doubling one quantity always double another, and how can we tell?

5MTB connection

A bike’s drivetrain is a proportion machine. In a given gear, the rear wheel always turns the same number of times per pedal turn, so wheel turns, and distance, are proportional to pedal turns.

Riding at a steady speed, distance is proportional to time. But a ride’s total time including a 10-minute stop is not proportional: the stop is a starting amount.

The mathOn the trail
kThe gear ratio, or a steady speed
y = kxWheel turns = ratio × pedal turns
Passes through the originNo pedaling, no distance
Not proportionalCost with a fixed lift-ticket fee
